resources.string: Types in statements
The expression already knows how to pass its type up. Now the statement checks whether that type works for it.
In an assignment, the type on the right has to fit the variable. An int fits a float, with a coercion. A float doesn't fit an int, because the fractional part would be lost.
Which assignment does the checker reject? Tap it.
Look for a float going into an int.
x times 2 goes up as float, and n is int. As in Java, that's an error. In the second one, the int becomes a float and passes.
In an if or a while, the condition has to be bool. Our language works like Java here: a number is not a condition.
Which condition does the checker reject? Tap it.
Which one goes up as int?
On its own, n goes up as int. C would accept it, but here the condition has to be bool. To test the number, compare it: n greater than zero.
In a call, each argument has to fit the parameter in the same position. In a return, the expression has to fit the type the function promises.
Which line does the checker reject? Tap it.
Check each argument against the parameter in the same place.
The first parameter is int, and x is float. The return of a plus b passes: the int becomes a float, as in the assignment.
Assignment, condition, call and return. In all of them, the statement compares the type that came up with the type it expects.
The block's DAG
Inside a basic block, the compiler can build a DAG. A DAG is a graph whose arrows never loop back.
Each leaf holds the variable's value on entry: b zero and c zero. Line one's sum becomes a node with two children. The node gets the name a.
Line two computes a minus d. It uses a's node, which already exists, and a new leaf, d zero.
Line four also computes a minus d. Which line already computed that value? Tap it.
Look for the same operation, with neither a nor d changing in between.
Between the two, neither a nor d changed. The minus node gets one more name, d, and no new node is born.
Now the minus node has two names: b and d.
And line three, c equals b plus c? Does it repeat line one's operation?
Yes: it's the same b + c
No: b changed on line 2
No: c is on the left
Look at what line two did to b.
Same text, different value. b is now the minus node. So line three's plus is a new node.
Four lines, three operations. Line four becomes just d equals b, with no operation at all.
The DAG only merges nodes with the same operator and the same children. That's how it finds the common subexpression.
Live in the loop
This is the sum loop in three-address code. The liveness you saw went bottom-up, in a block without jumps.
A variable is live if someone will still read its value. In a loop, what comes after the goto is up at the top.
After i receives t3, which line reads i first? Tap it.
Follow the goto. It goes back to the loop's label.
The goto goes back, and the loop test reads i. So i is still live at the end of the body.
Who is live after i receives t3?
After that line comes the goto, and it leads back to the test.
The test reads i and n, and the body will still read s. All three stay live.
The goto doesn't fall to the line below. So the analysis repeats its passes until nothing changes. Here, two change something, and the third only confirms.
At the top of the loop, i, n and s are live together. In the graph, the three fight, and each one needs its own register.
A common mistake: writing the parent before the children. Here is the same MIPS with the blocks swapped.
Parent before children
Which line reads a value that hasn't been stored yet? Tap it.
Look for tmp1. Which line stores it?
Only the last line stores tmp1. That's why the generator visits the children first.
Now another tree: a times b plus c. The times is on the left now. Build the MIPS in the right order.
